claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the interplay between the thermodynamic driving force for decomposition and kinetic barriers to atomic rearrangement.
A critical temperature exists at which a composition-dependent free-energy difference exceeds the effective barrier to formation of a secondary phase.
The secondary phase may be FCC or an intermetallic precipitate.
Slow atomic diffusion kinetically constrains phase separation in this alloy.
Local compositional fluctuations and atomic segregation at grain boundaries or within the matrix act as nucleation sites for the secondary phase.
Within a specific thermal regime, the emerging phase has lower free energy than the BCC state, providing a thermodynamic drive for phase separation.
Restricted atomic diffusion delays the transition from BCC to the secondary phase.
A temperature regime that provides sufficient atomic mobility while retaining a strong thermodynamic driving force enables nucleation and growth of the secondary phase.
Nucleation and growth of the secondary phase destabilize the original BCC structure.
Samples aged at the critical temperature will progressively form a detectable secondary phase over time.
Samples aged well below the critical temperature will undergo minimal transformation and largely retain the BCC structure.
At the low-temperature baseline, kinetic constraints prevent significant phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism is limited to a narrow thermal regime in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 and may change for substantially different compositions.
